title: US Loses Measles Elimination Status After 26 Years as Cases Pass 5,400
excerpt: PAHO ruled on November 17 that measles has circulated uninterrupted in the United States for more than a year. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status in the same announcement.
body:
• The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced on Tuesday, November 17, that the United States has lost the measles elimination status it held since 2000, after the virus circulated uninterrupted for more than 12 months.
  • The CDC counted 5,412 confirmed US cases in 2026 as of November 12 — the most in any year since 1991 — after 2,289 cases in 2025; 96% of infections were in people unvaccinated or of unknown vaccination status, according to STAT.
  • State health departments have reported 10 measles-associated deaths this year, according to STAT, while the CDC's national page lists six and says its figure is subject to change. Mexico and Bolivia also lost elimination status; Canada lost its last year.
  • For families: the CDC schedule is a first MMR dose at 12 months and a second at 4 to 6 years, and doctors can give infants an extra dose from 6 months in areas with an active outbreak, according to Science News.

Measles is endemic in the United States again. The Pan American Health Organization declared on Tuesday, November 17, that the country has lost its measles elimination status, a designation it had held since 2000, after analyses showed the virus spreading uninterrupted for more than a year from the first outbreak in West Texas in 2025, according to Science News. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their elimination status in the same announcement, PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa said at a news conference; Canada lost its status in 2025.

The decision is a formal recognition of transmission that has already happened. It does not change vaccine recommendations or school rules, but it is the international health system's judgment that the United States can no longer show it stops measles chains of spread inside its borders.

What elimination means, and how it was lost

A country holds elimination status when it prevents persistent spread of the virus. Imported cases can still occur, and limited transmission can follow, but if those chains are not stopped within a year, measles is considered endemic again, STAT reported. PAHO's reverification commission reviewed a period starting in January 2025 and based its finding on a series of cases continuing for at least 12 months.

"Elimination must be continuously protected."

— Jarbas Barbosa, Director, Pan American Health Organization, via STAT

"Losing measles elimination status is a tragic loss for our country," Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer for the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials, told reporters on Monday, according to STAT. "Measles has taken a hold in our country."

The numbers behind the decision

The CDC's measles page, updated November 13, counted 5,412 confirmed cases in the United States in 2026 as of November 12, reported by 47 jurisdictions, with a further 18 cases among international visitors. The agency counted 43 new outbreaks this year and said 96% of confirmed cases were outbreak-associated; 591 people, 11% of cases, were hospitalised. Pennsylvania has reported the most cases of any state this year, followed by South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin.

Last year's total of 2,289 cases was itself the highest since 1991, according to CDC data cited by STAT, and the overwhelming majority of infections — 96% — are in unvaccinated people or people whose vaccination status is not known. On deaths, the tallies differ by source: state health departments have reported 10 measles-associated deaths this year, according to STAT, while the CDC's page lists six and notes the figure is subject to change. New York and Wisconsin have each reported their first measles deaths in at least 30 years, STAT reported.

Why the virus found room

Coverage has slipped below the level that smothers transmission. About 95% of a community needs to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks, Science News reported, but roughly 92% of US kindergarteners had received the MMR vaccine in 2025, down from 95% in 2019, according to the CDC. At state level, kindergarten coverage has dropped below 90% in nearly 20 states, according to STAT.

The federal response, so far, has rested largely on money and state efforts. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said on Tuesday that the agency is "focused on stopping outbreaks" and has invested $100 million in state and local health departments, according to STAT. "The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," she said. The CDC's November 17 statement said it would "encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection," according to Science News.

What happens next

Regaining the status is possible, but slow. A country must stop ongoing outbreaks and then show that no one caught measles within its borders for a full year, Science News reported, and PAHO expects the United States, Mexico and Bolivia to submit corrective plans in the coming weeks. Venezuela and Brazil both regained elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019, following extensive vaccination campaigns.

For Indian families in the United States — and for relatives visiting from India, whose arrivals account for some imported cases nationally — the practical step is a records check, not alarm. The vast majority of Americans remain protected, and two MMR doses are the protection the CDC schedule is built on: the first at 12 months, the second at 4 to 6 years. In an area with an active outbreak, doctors can move earlier, giving infants an extra dose from 6 months and the second dose a month after the first, according to Science News. State health departments carry the most current local case information.
